newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Focus - G10 central banks upbeat on economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: Focus - G10 central banks upbeat on economic outlook.

text.p: Central bank governors from the Group of 10 (G10) industrialised nations gave an upbeat assessment for economic growth in North America, Europe and Japan on Monday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said.
Prospects remain good for the United States and Canada to keep growing without sparking inflation, they agreed at a monthly meeting at the Bank for International Settements (BIS).

Tietmeyer, who is chairman of the panel, added that fears that Japan's fiscal policy could crimp growth in the world's second-biggest economy have also faded, while many countries in Europe are showing signs of a cyclical recovery from recent weakness.
Tietmeyer spoke to reporters after the meeting, which included briefings by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen.

"I think both countries have all in all a relatively positive outlook as far as growth is concerned and as far as no inflationary growth is concerned," he said of the North American neighbours. He did not elaborate.
Tietmeyer said fears that Tokyo's economic policies could hurt growth had also subsided.
"We had a new assessment (of the Japanese economy)...fears that fiscal drag could have big negative impact seemed to be less now than before," Tietmeyer said.
Tietmeyer said G10 governors saw improved growth in continental Europe in the first quarter of 1997.
"One can see some improvement as far as growth in the first quarter, but of course the situation is different from country to country, no doubt about that," Tietmeyer said.

"We also feel cyclical improvement -- if it continues -- is one important element, but that further structural adjustment is necessary for improving the employment situation and reducing unemployment," he said.
Tietmeyer has often stressed the need to make European labour markets more flexible as a tool to reduce double-digit jobless rates on the continent.
Structural adjustments would also bolster investor confidence, something he said that was necessary in many continental European countries.
Tietmeyer said G10 central bank governors had discussed currency exchange rates at the meeting, but he had nothing to say about what markets were doing.
"We of course discussed it (exchange rates) but I can add nothing," Tietmeyer said. He specifically declined to comment on the recent decline in the dollar against major currencies.

Tietmeyer said G10 central bank governors, at their first meeting since British elections on May 1, found it interesting that Britain's new Labour government had given the Bank of England power to set interest rates.
He said Bank of England Governor Eddie George had detailed for the group the changes that new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown had made.
"The chancellor has elaborated clearly that the interest is to break with the short-term orientation and to move to a longer-term orientation of monetary policy," Tietmeyer said.
"This is in my view and the view of the (G10) colleagues a very interesting argument because it comes from the United kingdom," he added. He did not elaborate.
Despite its name, the G10 groups 11 countries -- Belgium, Britain, Canada, France, Germany. Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States.
